summary: Background: Nutritional problems are common during colorectal cancer (CRC) treatment and recovery; digital technologies may extend nutrition care beyond clinical visits. Intermittent care may miss intake, symptoms, and nutritional status; prior reviews addressed broader digital health or mobile app interventions rather than monitoring-informed CRC nutrition management. Objective: This review evaluated intelligent digital monitoring–supported nutrition management with respect to anthropometric outcomes, nutritional status, dietary intake, quality of life, and nutrition-related biochemical markers in adults with CRC. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, CENTRAL, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, and SinoMed from inception through June 30, 2026. Eligible interventions required repeated nutrition-related data collection, digitally traceable recording or transmission, and data-informed feedback or action. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), nonrandomized comparative studies, prospective cohorts, and prospective single-arm studies. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) and ROBINS-I (Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions) tools. Comparable RCTs were pooled using random-effects models; all other studies were synthesized narratively. Evidence certainty was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Results: Ultimately, 14 unique studies from 15 reports (2617 participants), including 7 RCTs, were included; 9 were conducted in China. All RCTs had some concerns; 5 of 7 nonrandomized studies had serious risk of bias. Body weight was synthesized narratively. Patient-Generated Subjective Global Assessment (PG-SGA) scores were lower than in controls (3 RCTs; n=244; mean difference [MD] −1.50, 95% CI −1.85 to −1.15; moderate certainty). Primary analysis showed higher energy intake (2 RCTs; n=138; MD 204.30 kcal/d, 95% CI 191.57 to 217.04; very low certainty), but this finding was not robust in a post hoc small-sample sensitivity analysis (95% CI −379.28 to 787.88; =.14). Effects were unclear for BMI (3 RCTs; n=305; MD 0.82 kg/m², 95% CI −0.27 to 1.90; low certainty), protein intake (2 RCTs; n=138; MD 20.16 g/d, 95% CI −37.39 to 77.72; ²=74%; very low certainty), quality of life (3 RCTs; n=188; MD 16.82, 95% CI −14.62 to 48.26; ²=95%; very low certainty), albumin (2 RCTs; n=188; MD 4.75 g/L, 95% CI −36.48 to 45.98; ²=98%; very low certainty), and hemoglobin (2 RCTs; n=188; MD 9.36 g/L, 95% CI −104.87 to 123.59; ²=95%; very low certainty). Conclusions: Intelligent digital monitoring–supported nutrition management may improve nutritional status, but effects on energy intake and other outcomes remain uncertain. Monitoring should complement, not replace, professional nutritional assessment and individualized care. Few trials, risk-of-bias concerns, heterogeneity, and geographic concentration limit conclusions; larger multicenter RCTs with standardized outcomes and defined monitoring-feedback components are needed. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251218785; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251218785
title: Application of Intelligent Digital Monitoring for Colorectal Cancer Nutrition: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: Background: Health-promoting new media can extend access to health information and education in rural communities. However, services need to accommodate residents’ preferences for both communication features and practical requirements for use. Existing research on technology acceptance and disease-specific applications provides limited evidence about how rural residents weigh these features together when choosing services for general health promotion. Understanding these preferences can help guide locally appropriate digital service development. Objective: This study aimed to quantify rural residents’ stated preferences for functional attributes of health-promoting new media, explore preference variation, and identify priorities for services suited to rural community settings. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional discrete choice experiment in 3 townships in Guizhou Province, China, from August to October 2024. Adults with experience using new media were recruited through convenience sampling and completed face-to-face questionnaires. A literature review, expert consultation, and resident focus groups identified 6 attributes: operation mode, device type, information content, experience, information source, and daily time investment. The questionnaire was pretested with 20 residents before the main survey. Investigators provided standardized explanations and visual aids when needed to support comprehension. The experimental design included 24 choice tasks divided into 3 blocks. Each respondent completed 8 tasks, selecting between 2 hypothetical service profiles without an opt-out option. Conditional logit models estimated average preferences using respondent-clustered SEs. We report coefficients and 95% CIs. Daily time investment was modeled categorically, with 1 hour per day as the reference. Mixed logit models explored preference heterogeneity. Participants provided written informed consent. Results: The analysis included 327 respondents who contributed 2616 choice occasions; 247 (75.5%) were women and 208 (63.6%) were aged 41 to 50 years. Most respondents had primary school education or below (n=198, 60.6%) and an annual household income per capita of ≤10,000 RMB (RMB 1=US $0.14035 as of October 31, 2024; n=194, 59.3%). Participants preferred voice or click operation over typing (β=−0.18, 95% CI −0.25 to −0.11), mobile phones over professional devices (β=−0.20, 95% CI −0.28 to −0.13), and basic over personalized content (β=−0.17, 95% CI −0.25 to −0.09). Daily time preferences were nonmonotonic: compared with 1 hour per day, 3 hours per day had lower utility (β=−1.06, 95% CI −1.52 to −0.60), whereas 5 hours per day had higher utility (β=0.25, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.34). Average preferences for experience and information source were not statistically significant. Supplementary mixed logit models yielded similar average preference estimates. Conclusions: Mobile delivery, voice or click operation, and basic health information were preferred features among participants in this study. These findings identify priorities for developing and evaluating health promotion prototypes in comparable communities. The nonmonotonic time pattern requires further investigation, and stated preferences should be evaluated against observed use. Convenience sampling limits the transferability of these findings to other rural populations.
title: Functional Preferences for Health-Promoting New Media Among Rural Residents: Cross-Sectional Discrete Choice Experiment

summary: Background: Dietary habits are strongly associated with a wide range of health outcomes. Although professional interventions are effective, they are resource-intensive. Digital health apps provide a low-cost alternative, and accumulating evidence suggests their potential to improve health behaviors and outcomes. In Japan, some apps are covered by public health insurance; however, evidence from real-world use, particularly regarding both health outcomes and health care expenditures, remains limited. Objective: This study aims to examine the relationship between the use of an automated diet management app and individual health outcomes, as well as health care expenditures, with a particular focus on the frequency of dietary self-monitoring behavior. Using real-world data from Japanese employees in a corporate setting, the study also seeks to provide evidence on the potential economic implications of digital health interventions and to provide evidence relevant to potential behavioral mechanisms underlying their effectiveness. Methods: We constructed individual-level panel data (2021‐2022) by linking app usage records, health checkup records, and medical claims records obtained through a health insurance association in a large Japanese corporate group. The main explanatory variable was the average number of daily meal records over the 90 days preceding the health checkup. We estimated the associations using fixed-effects panel models to control for time-invariant unobserved individual characteristics. Subgroup analyses by sex, age group, and baseline metabolic status were conducted to explore heterogeneity. Linear quantile regression was used as a supplementary analysis. Results: More frequent use of the app was associated with a lower BMI among men (β=−0.126 kg/m², 95% CI −0.22 to −0.04; =.001) and among women (β=−0.372 kg/m², 95% CI −0.54 to −0.20; =.001). Among men, app use was also associated with improvements in waist circumference, blood pressure, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, whereas among women, it was associated with lower probabilities of metabolic syndrome and abnormal blood glucose. Associations with BMI were stronger among users aged ≤40 years and those with poorer baseline health. In contrast, among users aged ≥50 years, improvements were observed primarily in cardiometabolic risk factors rather than BMI. No statistically significant association was observed for short-term health care expenditures. Sensitivity analyses yielded generally consistent findings for the primary outcomes. Conclusions: The findings suggest that digital diet management apps may contribute to statistically significant but modest improvements in health outcomes in workplace settings. However, given the observational nature of the study, the results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. Overall, the findings highlight the potential of digital diet management apps as scalable interventions and underscore the importance of promoting sustained engagement and targeting populations most likely to benefit.
title: Automated Diet Management App Use and Health Outcomes in Japanese Employees: Panel Data Analysis

summary: Background: Tobacco use remains a major global public health challenge, with a disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries. China, with the largest smoking population worldwide, faces additional challenges in smoking cessation due to sociocultural factors such as limited depth of risk awareness and strong social norms supporting smoking. Mobile health (mHealth) interventions, particularly smoking cessation apps, offer scalable and accessible support for behavior change. Limited qualitative research explores how Chinese smokers perceive smoking cessation apps and their roles in supporting quitting. Objective: This study aims to explore Chinese smokers’ experience of using smoking cessation apps to support smoking cessation. Methods: Chinese smokers with experience using smoking cessation apps were recruited via purposive sampling through social media. In total, 24 semistructured interviews were conducted online in Mandarin, audio-recorded, and transcribed verbatim. Interview questions explored participants’ experiences of using smoking cessation apps, including their perceptions of different app features, factors influencing their engagement, and how these features supported or hindered their quit attempts. Qualitative analysis was conducted to identify themes related to participants’ experiences regarding smoking cessation apps. Results: Ten themes were identified through qualitative analysis. Smoking cessation apps were perceived as most effective for users who were motivated to quit and believed in the usefulness of the apps. Features such as progress tracking and feedback enhanced extrinsic motivation and self-efficacy, with potential to foster intrinsic motivation over time. However, engagement with apps could decrease as users became more confident in maintaining abstinence. Social support functions provided emotional and informational support, and interactions with other quitters generated positive competition, particularly for users experiencing social isolation, although engagement with these features varied. Relapse prevention components, such as withdrawal symptoms education and recording features, were infrequently used when support was perceived as generic, low intensity, or insufficiently actionable. Good usability and user experience design were key drivers of sustained engagement. Participants valued apps that were simple and intuitive while offering different content formats, although preferences varied between users. Participants also described generic and nonpersonalized support as a limitation, despite rarely explicitly requesting greater personalization. Conclusions: Smoking cessation apps may support quitting through multiple mechanisms, including enhancing motivation and self-efficacy and facilitating social support, but their perceived value and use depend on users’ needs, beliefs, and contexts. The findings highlight broader considerations for mHealth intervention design and evaluation, including interpreting engagement in relation to changing support needs, recognizing that social features may generate additional motivational mechanisms through peer interaction, providing actionable and responsive behavioral support, accommodating diverse user preferences while maintaining usability, and using co-design to identify underlying user needs that may not be explicitly articulated. These considerations may inform the development of more responsive and user-centered mHealth interventions for smoking cessation and other behavior change contexts.
title: Chinese Smokers’ Perspectives on Smoking Cessation Apps: Qualitative Descriptive Study

summary: Background: Mobile health (mHealth) apps for menstrual cycle and fertility tracking are widely used to support self-monitoring, reproductive planning, and health awareness among women. These tools also promise personalized predictions and convenient access to reproductive health information. Still, concerns persist regarding their clinical accuracy, adaptability to irregular cycles, algorithmic transparency, and real-world user experience. Objective: This structured review aimed to evaluate the features, physiological integration, predictive performance, validation practices, and user-reported outcomes of mobile apps designed for menstrual and fertility tracking, and to contextualize the current evidence using the COSMIN (Consensus-based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments) and ISPOR (International Society for Health Economics and Outcomes Research) evaluation frameworks. Methods: A structured narrative review of studies evaluating mobile apps for menstrual cycle and fertility tracking was conducted. Literature published between January 2013 and October 2025 was identified through searches of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by semantic and citation-based searches in Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, and Google Scholar. AI-assisted prioritization was used only to support screening efficiency, whereas human reviewers performed all eligibility decisions and data verification. Forty studies met the predefined eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. Because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, outcomes, and validation methods, no meta-analysis was performed. Results: Of the 40 included studies, most were observational and relied on self-reported data from a predominantly high-income, technologically literate population. Twenty-four apps incorporated physiological inputs, such as basal body temperature, luteinizing hormone measurements, or wearable-derived metrics, whereas others relied primarily on calendar-based predictions. Multiparameter and sensor-augmented approaches generally demonstrated higher agreement with biological or clinical reference standards than calendar-only methods, with selected studies reporting fertile-window prediction accuracies approaching 85% to 90% under optimal adherence conditions. However, only a small subset of apps has reported formal clinical validation or regulatory clearance. User satisfaction was strongly associated with perceived accuracy, personalization, and usability, whereas inaccurate predictions, particularly among users with irregular cycles, were linked to frustration, anxiety, and high attrition. Conclusions: Menstrual and fertility tracking apps that integrate physiological signals outperform calendar-based approaches in terms of predictive performance; however, robust clinical validation, transparency, and inclusivity remain limited. Reported accuracy metrics should be interpreted cautiously because real-world adherence, irregular cycle patterns, and algorithmic bias substantially affect reliability. These tools are best positioned as decision-support and self-awareness technologies, rather than as autonomous diagnostic instruments. Future evaluations should apply standardized frameworks, such as COSMIN and ISPOR, explicitly communicate uncertainty, and prioritize diverse and irregular-cycle populations to ensure equitable and clinically meaningful digital reproductive health solutions.
title: Mobile Apps for Women’s Physiology Tracking: Structured Narrative Review

summary: Background: When trying to intervene early to prevent manic episodes, clinicians are hindered by patients underreporting their symptoms as they are becoming hypomanic or manic (ie, emerging symptoms). Continuous passive monitoring using wearable technology offers a potential solution to address this problem by capturing behavioral signals that do not depend on self-awareness. However, its clinical usefulness requires validation before implementation. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate whether passively collected wearable data can detect hypomanic symptoms using an explainable machine learning framework. Methods: We applied explainable machine learning to densely sampled multimodal data from a 2-year observational study of digital monitoring in 178 patients with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder (mean follow-up 540 days; range 120-706 days). Data on activity and sleep were collected continuously using wearable technology. Self-reported data were collected daily on their mood, energy, and anxiety, and weekly using the Altman Self-Rating Mania Scale (ASRM). To identify robust digital markers of hypomanic symptoms, we analyzed 252 time- and frequency-domain features from 43 participants who experienced at least 1 ASRM-defined symptomatic interval. Results: Passively collected data achieved high accuracy, comparable with daily self-reported data in detecting symptomatic intervals (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.91 vs 0.93, respectively). Combined daily passive wearable data features achieved higher sensitivity (92.0% vs 85.4%), balanced accuracy (0.90 vs 0.89), and stronger rule-out usefulness (negative predictive value 97.8% vs 96.1%) than self-report data, with daily sleep features alone driving most of this signal (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.91, sensitivity 91.8%). The high classification performance using wearable data was explained by reductions in spectral entropy and flux across domains, reflecting a decreased complexity and variability in mood, activity, and sleep patterns, consistent with a shift toward pathologically stable states. Conclusions: Passive monitoring using wearable technology can detect hypomanic symptoms with high accuracy, supporting its potential as a clinically meaningful tool for continuous, objective monitoring in patients who underreport hypomanic symptoms. These findings are associative and concurrent in nature; they do not establish predictive validity. Prospective studies are needed to evaluate predictive validity for early detection of ASRM-defined symptomatic intervals.
title: Passive Monitoring for Detecting Hypomanic Symptoms in Bipolar Disorder Using Explainable Machine Learning: Longitudinal Observational Study

summary: Background: Health anxiety (HA), classified in the ) under illness anxiety disorder (IAD) or somatic symptom disorder, is an increasingly prevalent condition associated with substantial psychological and health care burdens. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) offer scalable and accessible approaches to care, with digital behavioral interventions (DBIs), particularly internet-delivered cognitive and behavioral therapies, among the most frequently studied. However, their effectiveness in reducing HA has not been comprehensively synthesized. Objective: This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effectiveness of DBIs for reducing HA in adults and to examine their effects on related psychological outcomes. Methods: This systematic review and meta-analysis followed the PRISMA 2020 statement and Cochrane guidance. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to November 1, 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-experimental studies, and cohort studies involving adults with HA. HA severity was the primary outcome. Random-effects meta-analyses were restricted to RCTs. Methodological quality was appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute tools, risk of bias in RCTs using Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2), and certainty of evidence using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE). Results: Sixteen studies involving 2581 participants were included, comprising 9 RCTs, 6 quasi-experimental studies, and 1 cohort study. Six RCTs involving 585 participants contributed to the primary meta-analysis. Digital interventions significantly reduced HA compared with control conditions (Hedges =−0.77, 95% CI −1.25 to –0.30; =.002), although between-study heterogeneity was substantial (²=86.7%). Leave-one-out analyses showed that this effect remained significant after exclusion of any individual trial. By contrast, pooled effects on illness-related attitudes, general anxiety, anxiety sensitivity, and depressive symptoms were not statistically significant and were characterized by substantial heterogeneity. Among the 9 RCTs, 4 were judged as having low overall risk of bias, 2 had some concerns, and 3 were at high risk. GRADE certainty was low for HA and very low for the secondary outcomes. Conclusions: Digital interventions show potential for reducing core health-anxiety symptoms, but confidence in the magnitude and generalizability of the effect is limited by substantial heterogeneity, risk-of-bias concerns, and low certainty of evidence. Evidence for broader psychological outcomes remains inconclusive. Adequately powered, well-reported RCTs using rigorous outcome assessment, appropriate active comparators, and longer follow-up are needed to confirm effectiveness and clarify which patients benefit most and under what delivery conditions. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251238746; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/
title: New Insights and Effectiveness of Digital Interventions for Health Anxiety: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: Background: Mobile health (mHealth) apps for weight and glycemic control support self-monitoring and behavior change, but engagement often declines over time. Although relapse in diet and exercise is common, little is known about how users experience relapse within digital contexts or how apps should respond. Objective: This study aimed to explore how users of mHealth apps for weight and glycemic control experience, manage, and wish to be supported during dietary and exercise relapses. Methods: A descriptive qualitative design was adopted. Semistructured online interviews were conducted with 26 adults who had used weight or glycemic control apps for at least 3 months and reported at least 1 relapse. Data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Results: Seven themes emerged: stress and reduced capacity as conditions surrounding relapse; cultural, temporal, and environmental misalignment; psychological disengagement and avoidance; social and relational influences; relapse as emotional disengagement rather than simply a behavioral lapse; informal relapse management and self-directed recalibration; and desire for compassionate, context-aware support. Participants described relapse in relation to stress, grief, caregiving and occupational demands, religious observances, festivals, shift work, travel, and constrained food environments. Relapse was frequently experienced as emotional disengagement, characterized by guilt, shame, identity threat, and loss of meaning, and was often accompanied by avoidance of the app or monitoring devices. Participants managed relapse through self-directed strategies such as temporal resets, goal adjustment, partial engagement, and social support, but reported few structured relapse-recovery tools within apps. They expressed a strong preference for flexible goals, context-aware modes, mood-sensitive feedback, neutral language, and gentle reentry pathways. Conclusions: Participants’ accounts suggest that relapse in mHealth contexts involves emotional responses, contextual constraints, and changing self-management capacity. Flexible goals, neutral feedback, context-sensitive support, and graded reentry are promising design targets for relapse-responsive apps, but their effects on engagement and clinical outcomes require prospective evaluation.
title: Dietary and Exercise Relapse Management in Mobile Health Apps for Weight and Glycemic Control: Descriptive Qualitative Study

summary: Background: Skin cancer incidence is rising globally, increasing pressure on dermatology services and making efficient triage increasingly important. AI-driven skin cancer mobile health apps may help address this need, but their usefulness depends on whether users trust the advice and intend to follow it. Teledermatologist supervision has been proposed to combine AI efficiency with human clinical oversight, but dermatologist shortages make it critical to understand whether such supervision improves patient trust and adherence at the population level, or whether AI-only advice suffices for most users. Objective: This study tests whether teledermatologist supervision in an AI-driven skin cancer app affects patient trust and adherence intentions, compared with AI-only advice, and whether these effects differ by motivational context and risk assessment level. Methods: The randomized controlled, online vignette experiment with repeated measures was conducted from May to June 2025 as a single-center study among Dutch adults via an academic hospital-based patient panel. Eligible participants were adult members of the Erasmus MC Digital Patient Panel invited by email; those not completing all 4 vignette trials were excluded from the analysis. Participants completed 4 simulated mobile app scenarios varying in advice source (AI-only vs hybrid teledermatologist and AI) and risk assessment level (high vs low). The primary outcomes were trust in the advice (0‐100 scale) and adherence intention (recoded 3-level ordinal scale). Mixed-effects models were used to analyze the data. Results: Of the 2707 patient panel members, 879 participated (response rate: 32.5%). Participants were aged 18 to 93 (mean 62.5, SD 12.64) years; 50.4% (n=443) were female, and 21.4% (n=188) had a history of skin cancer. Participants were randomly allocated to motivation conditions (concern: n=438 vs curiosity: n=441). Trust was higher for hybrid advice than AI-only advice (mean 76.9, SE 0.73 vs mean 65.7, SE 0.73; estimated difference 11.98; partial ²=0.22; <.001). The odds of adherence were 1.7 times greater with hybrid vs AI-only (odds ratio 1/0.59=1.7, 95% CI 1.28-2.22; <.001). High-risk assessments increased adherence (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 2.2-3.8; <.001), with a moderated effect by motivation (=.03), showing stronger adherence with concern vs curiosity. The effect of advice source on adherence was fully mediated by trust. Conclusions: Teledermatologist supervision of AI-based advice robustly increased patient trust and adherence intentions, particularly for high-risk assessments and concerned users. Our experiment is innovative in testing teledermatologist supervision in a population-level AI skin cancer app and in examining how motivational context shapes responses to advice. Unlike studies focused on postreferral teledermatology or chatbot-based advice, this study isolates the effect of hybrid AI-human advice in a store-and-forward screening context. These findings suggest that developers and health care implementers may consider integrating teledermatologist supervision to maximize patient trust of and adherence to advice, potentially improving triaging efficiency and safety. Trial Registration: Open Science Framework 64pjn; https://osf.io/64pjn
title: Effect of Teledermatologist Supervision in AI Skin Cancer Apps on Patients’ Trust and Adherence Intentions: Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: Background: Mobile health (mHealth) apps are increasingly incorporated into diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES) programs to improve access to behavioral and clinical support. Although digital DSMES interventions have demonstrated benefits for self-management and glycemic control, considerable variability exists in app use, and less is known about whether preintervention technology attitudes are associated with subsequent app use and related outcomes. Objective: This study examined whether baseline technology attitudes are associated with app use and whether app use is associated with diabetes self-care and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) among adults participating in a digital DSMES intervention. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of the Living Healthier with Diabetes randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Texas (2020-2022). The RCT included 3 study arms: virtual DSMES, smartphone app–based DSMES, and a combined intervention. Analyses were restricted to the 2 intervention arms with app access. Baseline technology attitude was assessed using a 4-item composite scale. App use was measured using 2 indices: a primary app use index derived from days per week, minutes per day, and overall 3-month usage, and a feature-use index summing use across 10 app functions. Outcomes included HbA1c and diabetes self-care. Multivariable linear regression and linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate associations after adjustment for intervention arm, age, gender, past month financial situation, and baseline outcome values. Results: Of the 189 participants enrolled in the primary trial, 129 randomized to the intervention arms with smartphone app access were included. Follow-up HbA1c and diabetes self-care data were available for 116 (89.9%) and 114 (88.4%) participants at 3 months and 117 (90.7%) and 116 (89.9%) participants at 6 months, respectively. More positive baseline technology attitudes were associated with greater app use at both 3 months (β=0.64, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.99; P<.001) and 6 months (β=0.78, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.17; P<.001) but were not associated with feature use. App use was not associated with HbA1c at 3 months but was associated with lower HbA1c at 6 months (β=−0.04, 95% CI −0.074 to −0.013; P=.005) and in longitudinal models (β=−0.04, 95% CI −0.074 to −0.006; P=.02). Greater app use was associated with higher self-care at 3 months (β=0.56, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.82; P<.001) and 6 months (β=0.38, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.62; P=.002) and remained associated with self-care in longitudinal analyses (β=0.44, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.68; P<.001). App and feature use did not change significantly between 3 and 6 months (P=.14 and P=.11, respectively). Conclusions: These findings suggest that preintervention technology attitudes are associated with greater app use within digital DSMES programs and that greater use of the app may represent an important pathway linking mHealth interventions with behavioral and clinical outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06370494; http://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT06370494
title: Associations Between Technology Attitudes, App Use, and Health Outcomes in a Diabetes Self-Management Education and Support Intervention: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
